prompt: At a fixed sample rate, you raise a sine oscillator by one octave. What happens to the number of samples spanning each cycle?

options.explanation: The sample stream has the same rate while cycles happen twice as often, so fewer samples fit in each.

options.text: It stays fixed because the hardware rate is fixed
options.explanation: The hardware fixes samples per second, not samples per oscillator cycle.

options.text: It must become a whole number
options.explanation: A cycle can span a fractional number of sample periods; phase tracking handles this.
Correct. The same number of samples per second is now shared across twice as many cycles.

workedExample: An octave doubles cycles per second. The hardware still supplies the same number of sample instants per second, so each oscillator cycle spans half as many sample periods.

link.title: Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)

prompt: You move an oscillator to a higher sample rate while keeping the requested pitch unchanged. How should its phase increment in cycles per sample change?

options.text: Increase, because more samples need more cycles
options.explanation: More sample instants share the same number of cycles per second, so each step must be smaller.
The same step at more samples per second would raise the pitch.
Correct. The same cycle progress per second is spread over more samples.
Changing the unit does not fix the rate dependency; the accumulator and waveform function must agree on units.

workedExample: Keep the number of cycles per second unchanged. More updates per second therefore need less cycle progress per update. Compute the increment using the actual hardware sample rate.

prompt: Oscillator code computes its increment assuming 48 kHz, but the hardware runs at 44.1 kHz. What happens to every requested note?

options.text: It plays flat by the same frequency ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Each sample advances the assumed step, but fewer steps occur per second.

options.text: It stays in tune because the note frequency is in the code
options.explanation: The code chooses progress per sample; the clock determines samples per second.

options.text: It plays sharp by the same frequency ratio
options.explanation: A slower clock takes fewer steps per second, lowering rather than raising pitch.
The rate mismatch applies the same scale error to every phase increment.

workedExample: The increment fixes progress per sample. With a slower actual clock, fewer such steps happen each second, so the oscillator runs slow. Read the sample rate from the driver rather than hard-coding the assumed rate.

prompt: A sound’s wavelength changes when it enters a medium where sound travels faster, while its frequency stays the same. Must the synth change the samples that generated the tone?

options.text: Yes: it needs a longer memory buffer for the longer wavelength
options.explanation: Wavelength is distance in the medium, not audio buffer length.

options.text: No: wavelength describes propagation; oscillator samples depend on timing, amplitude and phase
options.explanation: Correct. The medium changes the distance between wave cycles, not the digital cycle timing.

options.text: Yes: the sample rate must equal the speed of sound
options.explanation: Sample rate measures samples per second; sound speed measures distance per second.

options.text: No: wavelength and frequency are always independent
options.explanation: At a given propagation speed they are linked; the medium’s speed also matters.

workedExample: Separate the digital time sequence from the sound travelling in a medium. A faster propagation speed increases wavelength for a fixed frequency. No distance measurement is needed to generate the same oscillator samples.
